questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: How much process is owed before a deprivation
questions.learningObjective: Identify the two questions used to decide how much process is owed
questions.stem: A research permit allowing your crew to collect specimens is suspended with no notice of the reasons and no chance to respond, and you want to know what process is owed before the suspension takes effect.

options.text: A full hearing before an administrative law judge is always required before any permit suspension.
options.misconception: assumes a trial-type hearing is always required

options.text: Some opportunity to know the claims and to present a defence, unless the balance of interests shows a hearing can be postponed.
Notice alone suffices, because the permit is a privilege the agency may withdraw at will.
options.misconception: treats the permit as revocable at will

options.text: Nothing is owed, because the permit belongs to the agency rather than to the permittee.
options.misconception: denies that a permit can create a protected interest

questions.explanation: Process is measured by what is possible and by the balance of interests, so a suspension may proceed first if the agency's interest outweighs the permittee's. A trial hearing is not automatic.
questions.hint: Ask what is possible and what the interests are.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Termination of an entitlement with no prior hearing
questions.learningObjective: Identify the safeguards required before an entitlement is terminated
questions.stem: A field technician's stipend ends by agency letter, and the technician asks whether the Constitution required a hearing before the payments stopped.

options.text: No, because the payments were made under a grant program and grants may be ended at the funder's discretion.
options.misconception: treats grant funds as outside constitutional protection

options.text: No, because a hearing is only required before a physical taking of property.
options.misconception: confuses deprivation with physical taking

options.text: A pre-termination hearing was required, with notice of the reasons, an opportunity to be heard, and assistance where needed.
Yes, but only if the technician can show the termination was motivated by a discriminatory purpose.
options.misconception: adds a discrimination requirement to process review

questions.explanation: Ending a statutory entitlement without notice and an opportunity to respond deprives the recipient without due process. The adequacy of process turns on notice and an impartial decisionmaker.
questions.hint: Entitlements ending are deprivations.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What equal protection forbids and does not require
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish what equal protection forbids from what it leaves to discretion

stimulus.body: A state wildlife agency can afford only one helicopter hour per week for the whole survey season, and the aviation officer proposes to give those hours to the sites where the rarest species were recorded. You have been asked whether equal protection requires anything further.

questions.stem: What does the equal protection clause require of an agency's allocation of scarce research hours among differently situated field sites?

options.text: It forbids arbitrary discrimination, but it does not require the agency to treat differently situated sites identically.
It requires identical treatment of every site, because each site is a site.
options.misconception: assumes equal protection demands identical treatment

options.text: It requires the agency to conduct an environmental impact study before allocating any flight time.
options.misconception: imports a procedural review into equal protection analysis

options.text: It requires the agency to give the most popular sites the larger share of flight time.
options.misconception: invents a popularity test for equal protection

questions.explanation: Equal protection forbids arbitrary discrimination; it does not require identical treatment of differently situated parties. An agency may allocate scarce resources on a rational basis.
questions.hint: Different situations need not get the same treatment.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A neutral permit requirement and its group effect
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a neutral rule's group effects establish on their own
questions.stem: A permit rule applies the same paperwork to every applicant, but completion time is consistently twice as long for applicants with certain surnames, and you ask whether that disparity is itself a constitutional violation.

options.text: It is a violation, because any rule that produces a disparate outcome is unconstitutional.
options.misconception: equates disparate effect with a constitutional violation

options.text: It is a violation, because the agency knew the rule would have that effect before adopting it.
options.misconception: assumes knowledge of the effect is required for liability

options.text: It is not a violation, because the equal protection clause never applies to permitting decisions.
options.misconception: denies that permitting is state action

options.text: Not by itself, because a neutral rule with a group effect needs proof of discriminatory intent, unless it is a pretext.

questions.explanation: A facially neutral rule is judged on purpose, not effects alone, though a strong effect may show the rule is a pretext. Disparate impact alone is not a violation.
questions.hint: Effects alone do not prove intent.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What strict scrutiny requires of a classification
questions.learningObjective: State the demands strict scrutiny makes of a race-based classification
questions.stem: Explain what a reviewing court demands when a law classifies by race, and why the demands are stricter than for most other classifications.

answer.exemplar: A race-based classification is suspect, so the government must show that the law serves a compelling interest and is narrowly tailored to achieve it. The burden is the government's throughout, and a law that is not narrowly tailored, or that rests on a race-based stereotype, cannot be sustained.

questions.explanation: A race classification must serve a compelling interest and be narrowly tailored to it, and the government bears the burden. The standard is stricter because race-based rules risk reinforcing prejudice.
questions.hint: Compelling interest, narrow tailoring, government's burden.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What the demanding standard does to the presumption of validity
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of strict scrutiny on the presumption of constitutionality
questions.stem: A state programme limits field access to applicants who meet a rule the state says serves a compelling interest, and the opposing landowner asks what the presence of strict scrutiny does to the ordinary presumption that state laws are valid.

options.text: Nothing changes, because every law is presumed valid until it is shown otherwise.
options.misconception: assumes strict scrutiny leaves the default in place

options.text: The law is presumed valid until the government proves it is narrowly tailored.
options.misconception: puts the tailoring burden on the challenger

options.text: The usual presumption falls away and the government must justify the classification on its own showing.
The law is presumed unconstitutional unless the landowner shows a compelling interest.
options.misconception: reverses which party must show what

questions.explanation: Once strict scrutiny applies, the government must carry its burden on both the interest and the fit. A court does not supply the government's missing justification.
questions.hint: The burden moves to the government.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The middle standard applied to a quasi-suspect ground
questions.learningObjective: Identify the standard applied to a sex-based classification

stimulus.body: A state rule requires that only applicants of a particular sex may obtain a particular class of field certification. The agency defends the rule as substantially related to an important interest in field safety. A research team asks what standard the rule receives.

questions.stem: What standard does the rule described in the excerpt receive?

options.text: The rule gets strict scrutiny, because it turns on a personal characteristic of the applicants.
options.misconception: treats every personal classification as suspect

options.text: The rule gets intermediate scrutiny, because sex is a quasi-suspect ground, and the state must show a substantial relation to an important interest.
The rule gets rational basis review, because certification rules are administrative housekeeping.
options.misconception: treats administrative labels as decisive for the standard

options.text: The rule gets no review at all, because the agency's own expertise is conclusive.
options.misconception: makes agency expertise unreviewable

questions.explanation: Sex is a quasi-suspect ground, so the rule must be substantially related to an important governmental interest, with the state bearing the burden. That middle standard sits between the other two.
questions.hint: Quasi-suspect means the middle test.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What the challenger must show under the deferential standard
questions.learningObjective: State the challenger's burden under deferential review
questions.stem: A landowner challenges a state wildlife-hunting rule that restricts the season on reasons the state says protect breeding stock, and the landowner's lawyer asks what her client must actually establish.

options.text: That the state has no conceivable reason for the rule, and that the rule is irrational on its face.
options.misconception: demands proof the state lacks any conceivable reason

options.text: That the state acted improperly in purpose, because effect alone never suffices under deferential review.
options.misconception: collapses the challenger burden into a purpose inquiry

options.text: That the rule is substantially related to an important interest, because hunting rules affect land use.
options.misconception: applies the intermediate standard to ordinary regulation

options.text: That the rule is arbitrary or irrational, so that no conceivable set of facts supports it.

questions.explanation: Under deferential review the challenger must show the law is arbitrary or irrational, and the state need not justify the law with its own proof. Showing only that the rule seems unwise is not enough.
questions.hint: Arbitrary or irrational is the hurdle.

questions.topic: How much process is owed before a deprivation
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the process inquiry and the government's burden
questions.stem: Your team's access to a research plot is suspended on the day of arrival, and the counsel you consult wants the analysis in two steps. First identify what process is owed, then identify what the government must show to proceed without a hearing.

options.text: Process means some opportunity to be heard, and the government must show the balance of interests favors acting first.
Process means a hearing before a neutral magistrate, and the government must show the plot is private rather than public.
options.misconception: confuses process with the question of land ownership

options.text: Process means written reasons after the fact, and the government must show the suspension was temporary.
options.misconception: treats after-the-fact reasons as the required process

options.text: Process means nothing, and the government must show the suspension benefits the agency's schedule.
options.misconception: collapses the process inquiry into a convenience test

questions.explanation: The governing test has two parts: whether some process is possible and whether the balance of interests supports acting first. Convenience to the agency alone is not a sufficient justification.
questions.hint: Possibility first, balance second.

questions.topic: Termination of an entitlement with no prior hearing
questions.learningObjective: Identify the protections attaching to a research authorization
questions.stem: A park research authorization is withdrawn before the field season begins, and the research team wants to know what protections attach to that authorization.

options.text: None, because an authorization to conduct research is revocable at the discretion of the agency.
options.misconception: treats research authorizations as revocable at will

options.text: A hearing before an independent tribunal, because the authorization is a property right in the research.
options.misconception: assumes a fixed tribunal is always required

options.text: Notice of the reasons, an opportunity to respond, and a decision by someone impartial, before the authorization lapses.
Only a written record of the reasons, because pre-deprivation hearings are never required for licences.
options.misconception: denies that pre-deprivation process is ever required

questions.explanation: A research authorization can protect the holder's expectations and is ordinarily revoked with notice, an opportunity to respond, and an impartial decision. Post-hoc reasons alone do not substitute for process.
questions.hint: Notice, response, impartiality, and timing.

questions.learningObjective: Apply equal protection to differently situated fellowship programmes
questions.stem: Your institute plans to fund two fellowships, one for a graduate student in a molecular field and one for a student in a field that has historically drawn few applicants, and the dean asks whether equal protection constrains the choice.

options.text: It forbids arbitrary discrimination, but it does not require the fellowships to be awarded on identical grounds in every field.
It requires that the fellowships be awarded by the same criteria regardless of discipline, because both are fellowships.
options.misconception: demands identical criteria across unlike programmes

options.text: It requires that a historically underrepresented field always receive the larger share of funding.
options.misconception: turns past underrepresentation into an entitlement

options.text: It does not apply, because university funding decisions are private rather than governmental.
options.misconception: ignores the public funding element in the decision

questions.explanation: Equal protection forbids arbitrary discrimination by public bodies but does not require identical treatment of unlike programmes. A rational funding rule for differing fields is permissible.
questions.hint: Rational distinctions between different programmes are fine.

questions.topic: A neutral permit requirement and its group effect
questions.learningObjective: Identify what an unexplained group disparity establishes
questions.stem: A licensing rule for drone flights requires every applicant to file the same form, but the agency's review of applications from one region takes far longer than for others, and you ask what that disparity establishes on its own.

options.text: It establishes intentional discrimination, because the disparity is large and consistent.
options.misconception: treats a strong disparity as proof of intent

options.text: It establishes a violation of the equal protection clause, because the outcomes differ so much.
options.misconception: treats disparity of outcome as a violation by itself

options.text: It establishes nothing at all, because administrative review times are not state action.
options.misconception: denies that agency delay is state action

options.text: It establishes little on its own, because a neutral rule needs proof of discriminatory purpose, though it may support an inference of pretext.

questions.explanation: A neutral rule's disparate effects do not by themselves establish a violation; purpose must be shown. A pronounced unexplained disparity can support an inference of pretext.
questions.hint: Effects can support pretext; they do not prove purpose.

questions.learningObjective: State the standard and the burden for a race-based allocation

stimulus.body: A state agency proposes to reserve a fixed number of its field trainee positions for applicants from one racial group, and the agency's counsel asks you to describe the constitutional standard and the burden it must meet.

questions.stem: What should the memo say about the standard and burden described in the memo?

options.text: Strict scrutiny, with the agency required to show a compelling interest and narrow tailoring, and the burden is the agency's throughout.
Rational basis review, because the programme addresses a historical disparity in access to training.
options.misconception: treats a remedial purpose as making the rule deferential

options.text: Intermediate scrutiny, because the classification resembles those applied to sex-based quotas.
options.misconception: borrows the standard used for quasi-suspect grounds

options.text: No constitutional review, because the agency has discretion over who it trains.
options.misconception: insulates agency hiring decisions from review

questions.explanation: A racial classification receives the most demanding standard, and the government must show a compelling interest and narrow tailoring. A remedial purpose does not soften the standard.
questions.hint: Race triggers the strictest standard.

questions.topic: What the demanding standard does to the presumption of validity
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the presumption of constitutionality does not carry the day
questions.stem: A trial court upholds a race-based allocation of research grants without requiring the state to explain its reasons, and the losing applicant asks why the ordinary presumption of constitutionality did not carry the day.

options.text: Because the presumption applies only to laws that do not burden any protected group.
options.misconception: describes the presumption by its effect on burdens

options.text: Because once the demanding standard applies, the government must justify the law on a record it builds itself.
Because the presumption is repealed for every administrative rule.
options.misconception: extends the rule to all administrative action

options.text: Because a state may never rely on the presumption after it loses a case once.
options.misconception: invents a rule of one-strike estoppel for statutes

questions.explanation: The ordinary presumption helps the party with the burden; once strict scrutiny applies the government must build its own record of a compelling interest and narrow tailoring.
questions.hint: The presumption aids whoever bears the burden.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how intermediate scrutiny is applied to a sex classification
questions.stem: Explain how a court applies the middle standard to a classification based on sex, and what the government must show to sustain it.

answer.exemplar: A sex-based classification is reviewed under intermediate scrutiny: the government must show that the classification is substantially related to an important governmental interest. The court asks whether the justification is important and genuine, not whether it is compelling, and the government bears the burden of producing it.

questions.explanation: The middle standard asks whether the classification is substantially related to an important governmental interest, with the burden on the government. It sits between the other two.
questions.hint: Substantial relation to an important interest.

questions.topic: What the challenger must show under the deferential standard
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the deferential burden from purpose and bad faith claims
questions.stem: A landowner's grazing exclusion is challenged as irrational, and the reviewing magistrate asks what the landowner must persuade the court of before the rule falls.

options.text: That the state acted with the purpose of harming the landowner, and that the harm was intentional.
options.misconception: converts the deferential inquiry into a purpose inquiry

options.text: That the rule is substantially related to an important interest, because it affects land use.
options.misconception: applies the intermediate standard to ordinary regulation

options.text: That the state had no reason at all, and that the exclusion was made in bad faith.
options.misconception: demands both a no-reason showing and bad faith

options.text: That the rule is arbitrary or irrational and that no conceivable facts would support it.

questions.explanation: Under deferential review the challenger must show the rule is arbitrary or irrational, and the state need not offer any justification. Bad faith may support the claim but is not the standard.

questions.topic: How much process is owed before a deprivation
questions.learningObjective: Identify the governing test for a deprivation without a hearing

stimulus.body: A state parks department has decided to remove a researcher's field markers and close the site without hearing the researcher first. The memo you are asked to write should explain the governing test for such a deprivation.

questions.stem: What test should the memo identify as governing the deprivation described?

options.text: The test is whether the removal was consistent with the department's published priorities, which is all the department's discretion requires.
options.misconception: reduces the inquiry to the agency's own priorities

options.text: The test balances the possibility of some process against the balance of interests, and the department must justify acting without a hearing.
The test requires a hearing before any property is removed, with no exceptions for emergencies.
options.misconception: makes a hearing mandatory regardless of the circumstances

options.text: The test is irrelevant, because markers on public land belong to no one in particular.
options.misconception: assumes absence of ownership defeats any claim

questions.explanation: The governing test balances whether some process is possible against the competing interests, and the department must justify acting first if it wants to skip a hearing. Mandatory hearings and no review are both wrong.
questions.hint: Possibility and balance decide the case.

options.misconception: treats employment status as deciding the process claim

options.text: Only a hearing after the payments stop, because nothing is taken away until the money is recovered.
options.misconception: assumes no deprivation until money is repaid

A full trial before a jury, because the worker's payments are a contractual right.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a court decides how much process is owed
questions.stem: Explain how a court decides how much process is owed before the government may deprive someone of a protected interest.

answer.exemplar: The court asks whether some process is possible, then weighs the individual's interest in receiving an orderly hearing against the government's interest in acting promptly, and the likelihood that error would be corrected later. The outcome is a balancing judgment rather than a fixed formula, and the government must justify postponing the hearing.

questions.explanation: The court asks what process is possible and then balances the competing interests, including the value of later correction. The result is a flexible judgment, and the government bears the burden.
questions.hint: Possibility first, then the balance of interests.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the process owed when an appointment ends without a hearing
questions.stem: A park ranger's seasonal appointment ends without any notice of reasons and without a hearing, and the ranger asks what the Constitution requires in that situation.

options.misconception: excludes seasonal workers from constitutional protection

options.text: Timely notice of the reasons, an opportunity to be heard, and an impartial decision before the appointment ends.

options.text: The county must show the rule violates strict scrutiny, because it operates so unevenly.
options.misconception: treats uneven operation as a suspect classification

options.text: The county must show the agency's stated reason was untrue, which alone decides the claim.
options.misconception: treats falsity of the reason as the whole claim

options.text: The county must show discriminatory purpose, though the pattern may support an inference that the stated ground is a pretext.

questions.explanation: The county must show discriminatory purpose, and the unexplained pattern may support an inference that the documentation ground is a pretext. The inference supports, not replaces, proof.
questions.hint: Pattern suggests pretext; purpose must be proved.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What strict scrutiny requires of a classification
questions.learningObjective: Explain why settled practice does not establish narrow tailoring
questions.stem: A council's classification is challenged as suspect, and the chair asks what the government must show. Counsel replies that the justification is long-standing and widely accepted.

options.text: That is enough, because a settled practice shows the classification is narrowly tailored.
options.misconception: treats settled practice as proof of narrow tailoring

options.text: No, the government must show a compelling interest and narrow tailoring on a record of its own.
That is enough, because the classification has been applied without challenge for many years.
options.misconception: treats acquiescence as constitutional justification

options.text: No, because the classification must be struck unless the council proves it serves no conceivable purpose.
options.misconception: reverses the standard the demanding test applies

questions.explanation: Long-standing practice does not establish narrow tailoring, so the government must show a compelling interest and a necessary fit on its own record.
questions.hint: Reputation is not a record.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What the demanding standard does to the presumption of validity
questions.learningObjective: Explain the continuing burden of justification after a ruling
questions.stem: After a court applies the demanding standard and finds for the challenger, the government's counsel asks whether it must show more before any new rule may be enacted.

options.text: No, because a legislative body is not bound by the earlier judgment in a different case.
options.misconception: assumes the earlier judgment binds only the parties

options.text: No, because the government may simply re-enact the same rule with different wording.
options.misconception: assumes new wording cures an old defect

options.text: Yes, because the burden of justification rests with the government whenever the standard is demanding.
Yes, but only if the challenger moves for a new trial.
options.misconception: makes a new motion the condition of relief

questions.explanation: The burden of justification rests with the government whenever the demanding standard applies, so any new rule must come with the government's own showing. A new trial motion is not the trigger.
questions.hint: The burden follows the standard, not the judgment.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The middle standard applied to a quasi-suspect ground
questions.learningObjective: Compare the middle standard with the strict and deferential standards
questions.stem: Explain how the middle standard treats a classification based on sex, and how that treatment differs from the standard applied to race and from deferential review.

answer.exemplar: A sex-based classification is subject to intermediate scrutiny: the government must show that the classification is substantially related to an important governmental interest, and the burden of producing that showing is the government's. Race-based classifications face strict scrutiny, demanding a compelling interest and narrow tailoring, while ordinary rules face deferential review under which the challenger must show the rule is arbitrary or irrational.

questions.explanation: The middle standard demands a substantial relation to an important interest, with the burden on the government. Race draws a stricter and more demanding test, and ordinary rules get the most forgiving one.
questions.hint: Substantial relation, important interest, government's burden.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What the challenger must show under the deferential standard
questions.learningObjective: State the standard and burden for an irrationality challenge
questions.stem: A field rule is challenged as irrational, and the reviewing panel wants the two steps set out. First state the standard, then state who bears the burden.

options.text: Strict scrutiny, and the government bears the burden of showing narrow tailoring.
options.misconception: pairs the strictest standard with the wrong burden

options.text: Deferential review, and the challenger bears the burden of showing arbitrariness or irrationality.
Intermediate scrutiny, and the challenger bears the burden of showing no substantial relation.
options.misconception: pairs the middle standard with the wrong burden

options.text: No standard, and the burden is on the state to show the rule was reasonable.
options.misconception: invents a reasonableness test with a shifted burden

questions.explanation: Deferential review applies, and the challenger must show the rule is arbitrary or irrational. Heightened standards do not apply to an ordinary field rule.
questions.hint: Deference for the rule, burden on the challenger.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: How much process is owed before a deprivation
questions.learningObjective: Identify the framework applied when a hearing is said to be infeasible

stimulus.body: A state's wildlife agency wants to close a research area at the start of the season and says a hearing is not feasible because the field staff are already deployed. The memo you write should identify the framework the agency must work within.

questions.stem: What framework should the memo identify for the agency?

options.text: Some opportunity to be heard where possible, and otherwise a balancing of the competing interests, with the agency bearing the burden.
A full hearing, because feasibility is never a reason to deny process.
options.misconception: ignores the feasibility inquiry entirely

options.text: None, because the agency owns the land on which the research area sits.
options.misconception: treats land ownership as a blanket immunity

options.text: Any process the agency considers convenient, because scheduling is within its control.
options.misconception: makes process a matter of agency convenience

questions.explanation: The framework requires some opportunity to be heard where feasible and otherwise a balancing of interests, with the agency bearing the burden. Inconvenience is not a permissible reason to skip process.
questions.hint: Feasible process first; otherwise balance the interests.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Termination of an entitlement with no prior hearing
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a form satisfies the process requirement
questions.stem: A state student loan servicer ends a deferment benefit on a student's payment, and the servicer gives the student a form to fill in but no hearing and no chance to be heard.

options.text: That is enough, because a form is a hearing in a different form.
options.misconception: treats a form as the equivalent of a hearing

options.text: It is not enough, because notice of the reasons, an opportunity to be heard, and an impartial decision must precede the loss.
That is enough, because the student received the benefit only at the servicer's convenience.
options.misconception: denies the student any protected interest

options.text: It is not enough, but only if the student can point to a rule the servicer broke.
options.misconception: makes an error in application the test

questions.explanation: Ending a deferment benefit without notice of the reasons and a chance to respond deprives the student without due process. A form is not a hearing, and the question does not depend on proving a mistake.
questions.hint: A form is not a hearing.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What equal protection forbids and does not require
questions.learningObjective: Explain why equal protection leaves many classifications to ordinary judgment
questions.stem: Explain to a client why the equal protection clause forbids some classifications while leaving others to ordinary political judgment.

answer.exemplar: The clause requires that public classifications be non-arbitrary and non-invidious, so a decision must rest on a rational connection to a legitimate purpose rather than on prejudice. It does not require that every citizen receive identical treatment, because people in different situations can reasonably be treated differently, and it does not guarantee equal results in every group.

questions.explanation: The clause requires rational, non-arbitrary reasons and forbids invidious distinctions. Many ordinary distinctions remain for political judgment because situations differ.
questions.hint: Arbitrary and invidious are banned; the rest is judgment.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A neutral permit requirement and its group effect
questions.learningObjective: State the government's obligations in defending a neutral rule
questions.stem: A permit rule is written in identical terms for every applicant, and the challenger's expert can show that the rule, as administered, has excluded a protected group almost entirely. Counsel asks what the state must do to defend it.

options.text: Nothing, because the rule's text is neutral and neutral rules need no defence.
options.misconception: ignores that neutral rules may still be challenged

options.text: Nothing, because the group affected has no right to apply for the permit.
options.misconception: assumes the absence of a right to apply defeats a claim

options.text: Prove the rule is strictly tailored to a compelling interest, because the exclusion is so severe.
options.misconception: applies strict scrutiny to a facially neutral rule

options.text: Offer a genuine reason for the rule, and if the stated reason does not explain the exclusion, expect a pretext finding.

questions.explanation: A neutral rule is assessed on purpose, so the state must explain the disparity with a genuine reason. If its stated reason cannot account for the exclusion, it is a pretext.
questions.hint: A neutral rule still needs a genuine reason.
